Kinahan, aged 49, has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017. He has previously denied all charges against him. But what do we know about Daniel Kinahan, one of the most wanted men in the world, and his alleged leadership of the billion-dollar Kinahan cartel? https://www.dw.com/en/taliban-says-three.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MwiS Taliban officials accused Pakistan of targeting civilians Image: Shafiullah Kakar/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Pakistan conducted airstrikes on northeastern Afghanistan on Monday on what Pakistani security officials described as militant hideouts, resulting in some deaths. The two neighbors reported conflicting casualty tolls. The Taliban government in Kabul claimed that three people were killed as it accused Pakistan of bombarding "civilian homes," while the Associated Press news agency cited two unnamed Pakistani security officials as saying that 28 suspected militants were killed. Afghanistan's deputy government spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat said that the strikes took place in the Kunar and Paktika provinces. Fitrat wrote on X that one strike hit at around 3:00 am Monday (2230 UTC, Sunday) in Kunar's Nurgal district and "completely destroyed" a house, adding that three people were killed and four other members of the family were wounded. He said that two locations were also hit in the Paktika province, claiming that a shop and an unoccupied house were destroyed. There has yet to be an official statement from Pakistan on the strikes. The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm Image: Shafiullah Kakar/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Strikes follow last week's militant attack in Pakistan The reported strikes come after a suicide bombing and a 20-hour gun battle between militants and police on Friday, which took place at a district police headquarters compound in the Pakistani city of Kohat, situated near the Afghan border. At least 31 people, including 16 police officers, were killed in the attack. Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a local militant group linked to the jihadist group Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack. The Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have been tense since the Taliban returned to power in 2021. The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm after former South Asian allies engaged in their worst clashes in years in February. Pakistan declared that month that it was in an "open war” with Afghanistan , following a rise in militant attacks on civilians and security forces inside Pakistan. Afghanistan launched retaliatory strikes after Pakistan carried out airstrikes inside Afghan territory and the cross-border fighting has since claimed the lives of hundreds of people. Pakistan last mounted deadly airstrikes in Afghanistan in June. Islamabad accuses Afghanistan of sheltering militant groups which launch attacks inside Pakistan's territory. Main among these is the TTP, often referred to as the Pakistani Taliban and Baloch separatist groups from the border areas. The Taliban has dismissed ​the allegations, saying that militancy in Pakistan is an internal problem. Are Pakistan and Afghanistan heading for war? https://www.politico.eu/article/labour-u.text: LIVERPOOL, England — One of the most stinging criticisms thrown at Andy Burnham is that he is a people-pleaser who hates to pick a side. But on one of the most contentious issues facing Labour, he has done just that. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband made the shift clear in his speech to Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool this week — directly telling internal critics who had accused the governing party of failing to take strong enough action to defend Palestinians: “You were right.” Many of those internal critics now hope a shift in Labour policy — imposing trade sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank — will go some way to repair electoral damage done to the center-left party in recent years. Advertisement Advertisement But in addressing one of the most difficult fault lines in the party membership, Miliband has also sparked deep anger among some of his colleagues, particularly some Jewish Labour members, and charges of diplomatic recklessness. Miliband’s team has yet to respond to a request for comment on this piece. Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, was seen as flat-footed in his support for Gaza as Israel responded with force to the Oct. 7 2023 attacks, and slow in his decision to recognize Palestine. Under his leadership, constituencies with high Muslim populations turned away from the Labour Party in large numbers, either electing independents or preferring the Greens. But one of Miliband’s first acts as Burnham’s foreign secretary was to announce the sanctions — and accuse Israel’s government of turning a blind eye to the “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians by settlers. It was a dramatic escalation of the British government’s rhetoric. Jess Phillips, a Labour former minister who is the MP for Birmingham Yardley, said: “I think it’s a beginning of building back trust with the vast majority. “I wouldn’t say there is a ticker tape parade or anything but an opportunity for a fair hearing.” Emily Thornberry, the Labour chair of the cross-party Foreign Affairs Committee, said: “As far as I’m concerned, the only important consideration is that the government has finally done the right thing.” She told at the POLITICO Pub at party conference in Liverpool Tuesday: “If you’re a grown-up politician, you can say sometimes: ‘Well, we were wrong about that. We wished we’d listened to you.'” Advertisement Advertisement Even those on the left of the party who had been the most scathing about Labour’s approach to Gaza appear at least partly satisfied by Miliband’s actions — and think they have a message they can take back to angry voters. Labour MP Rachael Maskell said voters are “really engaging” with a policy shift which “is not about sides but values, and that is what people are latching onto.” With that in mind, Labour activists are now beginning to feel quietly optimistic about an upcoming by-election in Holborn and St Pancras, Keir Starmer’s former seat, where Labour had expected to face particular pressure from the Green Party over Gaza. “Because we have moved pretty much as far as we can now on Gaza — short of calling it a genocide — and that issue isn’t as dominating and fraught, we can talk about all sorts of issues and people feel up for listening,” said a Labour staffer. Green officials dispute that — believing their consistency on the issue will help get candidate (and Green Party Leader) Zack Polanski over the line. “I get the sense that people don’t trust Labour on the issue,” a Green Party councillor involved in by-election campaigning — granted anonymity to speak frankly — said. “Burnham and Miliband’s words are nice and all, but it’s a little bit too late. Greens have had a position stronger and longer.” The Miliband factor Despite earning party plaudits, Miliband has, for some, pushed beyond what is diplomatically wise. Advertisement Advertisement Three people described a meeting with the foreign secretary before the sanctions announcement, in which he was urged to wait until after the Israeli elections because of concern Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would weaponize the move. They said Miliband was intransigent and kept repeating that it was a “moral emergency.” The same people, who were granted anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions, said his refusal to wait forced them to conclude that his decision was partly influenced by the desire to announce the change in policy in time for the Labour conference and the by-election. Burnham has stood firmly behind the West Bank sanctions since they were announced, but it’s clear that they have been driven to a large extent by Miliband. The prime minister heaped praise on his foreign secretary in his own address to the conference Tuesday, insisting Britain would be “principled in our leadership in securing a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine, as Ed Miliband has shown.” A one-time Labour leader who carries more political clout than most on the government front-benches, Miliband has indeed chosen to make this fight intensely personal, describing himself as a “proud British Jew,” with the “deepest gratitude” to the state of Israel for giving refuge to his grandmother who lost her husband, Miliband’s grandfather, and 60 other family members at the hands of the Nazis. Miliband’s sanctions move was followed by allies in fellow middle powers, Canada and France, making similar moves, and one U.K. minister argued Britain had opened international conversations at the United Nations General Assembly that had been impossible before. For now, the British government is relieved that the feared blowback from Israel has been reasonably restrained. While Israel announced that the British consulate in Jerusalem will be closed as part of a retaliation, ministers were assured that intelligence cooperation will continue. Donald Trump, whose relationship with Netanyahu has wavered during their war in Iran, has appeared uncharacteristically calm about the sanctions. Advertisement Advertisement In Liverpool, some Labour MPs were still to be placated. Left-wing lawmaker Nadia Whittome told a Liverpool fringe event Tuesday night that Israel “needs to face a reckoning” — demanding that Britain impose a complete arms embargo and wider economic sanctions on the state. But for now, Miliband has at least made parts of the Labour faithful feel better about itself. MPs and party members making their way to the secure zone of the Labour conference in Liverpool have for years been confronted by demonstrations from pro-Palestinian protestors. “Ed said we were right,” one placard read on the Tuesday morning after his speech.

(Photo by Artur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images) WARSAW — The prime minister of Poland today used his keynote address at a security conference here to attempt to rally Europe to do more to combat what he said was the “real threat” from Russia. “No one wants escalation or war. We all dream of peace,” Donald Tusk said to an audience of European political, military and defense industry figures. “The path to peace does not lie through weakness. The path to peace lies in stopping the aggressor with all available means and forces.” Tusk said Russia would “not stop” with Ukraine and, given the chance, would seek to “reshape Poland’s security architecture” in a bid to “dismantle the security architecture in Europe so that Russian dominance returns to the state it was before 1989. We have no doubt about this.” Tusk said a new NATO “theory of victory,” revealed in a separate speech today by Supreme Allied Commander Europe Gen. Alexus Grynkewich left him “filled with optimism.” In Grynkewich, he said, he “had a partner who also harbors no illusions, no miconceptions, regarding Russia’s intentions toward Ukraine, as well as toward Europe and the entire world.” The prime minister said he was traveling to Brussels to call on Europe to increase pressure on Europe and toughen sanctions targeting Moscow. “Ukraine will not be broken or intimidated. Poland will not be broken or intimidated. Europe, NATO, and the entire free world will not be broken or intimidated. That message must go out today from every capital—from Warsaw to Washington,” concluded Tusk. Immediately following Tusk’s address, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy issued his own virtual address to the audience, saying that Moscow had launched attacks on Ukrainian cities despite US President Donald Trump’s claim that both sides had agreed not to strike energy targets. “If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people,” he said. Zelenskyy also claimed that recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers had diminished the amount of disinformation online — suggesting the centers had been used by Russian online provocateurs. A day after Trump announced a controversial oil deal with Russia, Zelenskyy implored the US to not give “concessions” but instead put “real pressure” on Moscow. To Poland, Zelenskyy said Warsaw and Kyiv were “natural allies.” “And when we stand together, Russia has no chance,” he said. “We need to end Russia’s war. We need to guarantee security.
